edits.why_correct: Financial abuse is a recognised form of abuse under the Care Act 2014, and her fear of her grandson's temper raises concern about her wider safety. The GP should listen, check whether she is in immediate danger, explore her wishes and follow local adult safeguarding procedures. Because she has capacity, she should be involved in decisions, although information can still be shared without consent if there is a serious risk to her or others. Source: Care and support statutory guidance (chapter 14, safeguarding), Department of Health and Social Care, Care Act 2014.

edits.why_wrong: B. A perianal abscess causes local pain, swelling and fever rather than obstructive symptoms. C. edits.why_correct: Long-standing transmural inflammation in Crohn's disease heals with fibrosis, narrowing the bowel lumen, most often in the terminal ileum. This produces recurrent post-prandial colicky pain, vomiting and distension from partial obstruction. Only mildly raised markers suggest a predominantly fibrotic rather than active inflammatory narrowing, which may need endoscopic dilatation or surgery. Source: Crohn's disease: management (NG129), NICE, 2019.

edits.why_correct: Fever, abdominal tenderness and worsening encephalopathy in a patient with cirrhotic ascites should be treated as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until proved otherwise. A diagnostic tap for neutrophil count, culture and other analysis is the key test, and British Society of Gastroenterology guidance advises a diagnostic tap in everyone with cirrhosis and ascites who is admitted, so that antibiotics can be started promptly if confirmed. Source: Guidelines on the management of ascites in cirrhosis, British Society of Gastroenterology and British Association for the Study of the Liver, 2020.

edits.why_correct: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when two of three criteria are met: characteristic abdominal pain, amylase or lipase at least three times the upper limit of normal, and typical imaging findings. She already has the biochemical criterion, so constant severe epigastric pain radiating to the back would complete the clinical picture and make imaging unnecessary for diagnosis. Source: Pancreatitis (NG104), NICE, 2018, with the revised Atlanta classification of acute pancreatitis, 2012.

edits.why_correct: Assessing food intolerance relies on identifying which foods precede symptoms, how soon after eating they start, and whether they are reproducible. A food and symptom diary is a practical way to capture this. This history guides any trial of exclusion and helps separate intolerance from allergy or other gut disease. Source: Food intolerance, NHS website (nhs.uk), accessed October 2026.

edits.pearl: In chronic liver disease a falling platelet count is a useful marker of advanced fibrosis and portal hypertension.
edits.why_correct: Cirrhosis raises pressure in the portal venous system, causing congestive splenomegaly. The enlarged spleen sequesters platelets (hypersplenism), so a gradually falling platelet count with a palpable spleen in liver disease is most likely due to portal hypertension. Reduced hepatic thrombopoietin production can contribute. Source: Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2018.

issues: Clinical update: why_correct/thinking/takeaway said testing is for transfusion before 1991 (start of UK donor HCV screening). Current NHS advice is to test anyone transfused in the UK before 1996; rewritten to 1996. Pearl's '>95% cure' changed to NHS wording (cures most people, 8-12 weeks of tablets). Added Source.

edits.why_correct: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne virus that becomes chronic in most people and can remain silent for decades while causing persistently raised transaminases. Current NHS advice is that anyone who had a blood transfusion in the UK before 1996 and has not been tested should be offered a hepatitis C test. Hepatitis C antibody testing with confirmatory RNA testing is appropriate, as curative antiviral treatment is available. Source: Hepatitis C (causes and treatment), NHS website, accessed October 2026.
edits.pearl: Hepatitis C is now treated with antiviral tablets taken for 8 to 12 weeks, which cure the infection in most people.

edits.takeaway: Persistently raised liver enzymes in someone transfused in the UK before 1996 should prompt testing for hepatitis C.

edits.why_correct: The liver is the commonest site of distant spread from colorectal cancer because venous blood from the bowel drains through the portal vein to the liver. Multiple lesions in both lobes, new deranged liver tests and weight loss in a man with previous bowel cancer make metastases most likely. He needs multidisciplinary review, as some colorectal liver metastases can be resected. Source: Colorectal cancer (NG151), NICE, 2020.

issues: Format only: added Source and sources. Content correct (albumin half-life about three weeks; PT/INR reflects short half-life clotting factors). Not a repeat of live BX221/BX222, as the time-course contrast is not tested there, though overlap is close - clinician may judge.

edits.why_correct: Albumin is made only by the liver and has a half-life of around three weeks, so a low level reflects reduced synthetic capacity over a longer period. This makes it useful for tracking chronic liver dysfunction, and it forms part of the Child-Pugh score. It can also be lowered by malnutrition, sepsis and protein loss, so it must be interpreted in context. Source: Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2018.

issues: Key was longest: lengthened A. Added Source (BSG 2018: prolonged PT/INR reflects impaired synthesis but can also be caused by vitamin K deficiency). Content correct.

options.A: Platelet sequestration within an enlarged spleen

edits.why_correct: The liver synthesises most clotting factors, including factors II, VII, IX and X. When hepatocyte function fails, their production falls and the prothrombin time lengthens. Failure to correct with vitamin K shows the problem is synthetic failure rather than vitamin K deficiency, which is why the INR is a key prognostic marker in liver disease. Source: Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2018.

edits.why_correct: Hereditary haemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder, most often due to homozygous C282Y HFE mutation, in which low hepcidin activity allows unregulated absorption of iron from the gut. The excess iron is deposited in the liver, pancreas, skin, heart, joints and pituitary, producing cirrhosis, diabetes and skin pigmentation. Source: Haemochromatosis, NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries; BSG guidelines on HFE haemochromatosis, 2018.

edits.why_correct: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of the ATP7B copper transporter, which impairs incorporation of copper into caeruloplasmin and its excretion into bile. Copper accumulates in the liver, then in the brain and cornea, causing hepatitis, psychiatric change and movement disorders in young people. Treatment is with a copper chelator such as penicillamine or trientine, or with zinc, which reduces copper absorption from the gut. Source: Wilson's disease, NHS website (nhs.uk), accessed October 2026.

edits.why_correct: Alcohol-related liver injury characteristically raises AST more than ALT, typically with a ratio of about two or more. Transaminases are usually only moderately raised, and GGT is typically high. Jaundice with tender hepatomegaly and fever in a heavy drinker, together with this pattern, supports alcohol-related hepatitis, whose severity is assessed with scores such as the Glasgow alcoholic hepatitis score. Source: Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2018.

edits.why_correct: Alkaline phosphatase comes mainly from the liver and bone. GGT is produced by the hepatobiliary system but not by bone, so a raised GGT alongside ALP indicates a hepatobiliary source, whereas a normal GGT points towards bone. This guides whether to pursue liver imaging or bone causes such as Paget disease. Source: Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2018.

options.D: Slower transit lets colonic bacteria make and absorb more ammonia

edits.why_correct: Colonic bacteria break down protein and urea to produce ammonia and other nitrogenous compounds. When transit slows, more of these are generated and absorbed, and a cirrhotic liver with portosystemic shunting cannot clear them, so they reach the brain. This is why lactulose, which speeds transit and acidifies the colon to trap ammonia, is the first-line treatment. Source: Rifaximin for preventing episodes of overt hepatic encephalopathy (TA337), NICE, 2015.
edits.correct_answer: D. Slower transit lets colonic bacteria make and absorb more ammonia

options.C: It alters gut function and sensitivity without damaging the bowel

edits.why_correct: Irritable bowel syndrome is a disorder of gut-brain interaction, involving altered motility and heightened visceral sensitivity without inflammation, ulceration or structural damage. Once the diagnosis is secure, it is not associated with a long-term increase in the risk of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Explaining this clearly is an important part of management and helps reduce anxiety. Source: British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on the management of irritable bowel syndrome, BSG, 2021; Irritable bowel syndrome in adults (CG61), NICE, 2008, updated 2017.
